request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
HOSPITAL COURSE:

Admission Date: April 29th, 2016
Discharge Date: N/A

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:

Ms. C, a 73-year-old woman with a history of uveal melanoma, was admitted to the hospital for epigastric pain and symptoms of gastric reflux following her second dose of ipilimumab as second line immunotherapy for liver metastases. She also had mild diarrhea with 3–4 loose stools daily. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy were performed to inform further treatment.

FINDINGS:

Esophageal, gastric and duodenal mucosa appeared normal on endoscopic examination without evidence of ulceration or other significant mucosal injury. Gastric biopsies exhibited lymphocytic inflammation surrounding pigmented cells scattered throughout the gastric mucosa. S100 and SOX10 immunostains confirmed multiple microscopic foci of melanoma with tumor associated inflammation resembling gastritis. Flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonic biopsies were normal.

HOSPITAL COURSE AND TREATMENT:

Glucocorticoid treatment was initially deferred as this was considered an appropriate antitumor response, and she received her third dose of ipilimumab. After the 3rd dose, she developed an elevation in her transaminases and bilirubin concerning for checkpoint hepatitis. She was started on glucocorticoids and further immunotherapy was held. Her hepatitis resolved on glucocorticoids. Her gastric symptoms also improved on glucocorticoid therapy consistent with an immune-mediated mechanism.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

Ms. C is advised to continue taking glucocorticoids and report any new symptoms to her healthcare provider. She is recommended to follow-up with her oncologist for further treatment options.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
CODE: C79

The episode was investigated for epigastric pain and reflux, and gastric biopsies confirmed multiple microscopic foci of melanoma in the stomach, which is secondary (metastatic) disease from her uveal melanoma. The gastritis-like inflammation was tumour-associated, so the established diagnosis is the gastric metastasis, which falls under C79 (secondary malignant neoplasm of other specified sites). The immune-mediated hepatitis and gastric symptoms were adverse effects of ipilimumab that were managed during the stay, but they were not the condition chiefly responsible for the admission.
